title: Cline CLI npm Package Compromised via Suspected Cache Poisoning Attack

reading.body:
An AI system deployed to triage GitHub issues accepted user input without sanitization or human review, allowing attackers to inject malicious prompts into issue titles. The AI would then execute these injected instructions, potentially running arbitrary code that could steal publishing credentials. This is a failure to isolate an AI system from sensitive operations and a failure to require human approval before deploying code changes.

The vulnerability persisted in Cline's GitHub Actions workflows from late December 2025 through February 9, 2026. It would have been caught by requiring human review of AI-generated code before it executed, or by preventing the AI system from accessing publishing credentials and cache systems. The researcher who discovered it reported the issue multiple times starting January 1st, 2026, but received no response until public disclosure triggered a fix within one hour.

It is not established whether the vulnerability was exploited to publish malicious code before it was patched. Evidence suggests an attempted exploitation may have occurred, but no confirmed malicious updates have been documented.

summary:
# Summary

Cline, an open-source artificial intelligence coding tool used by millions of developers, had a critical security vulnerability in its GitHub Actions workflows from late December 2025 through February 9, 2026. A researcher named Adnan Khan discovered that the AI-powered issue triage system allowed attackers to inject prompts into issue titles that could trick the AI into running malicious code. By combining this with a cache poisoning technique, an attacker could potentially steal publishing credentials and inject malware into Cline updates distributed through multiple platforms including the VS Code Marketplace and NPM.

The researcher reported the vulnerability multiple times starting January 1st, 2026, but received no response from Cline's team. After public disclosure on February 9th, the company fixed the issue within one hour by removing the AI workflows and eliminating cache usage in release pipelines. Evidence suggests someone may have attempted to exploit the vulnerability, though no malicious updates were confirmed. Cline later rotated all affected credentials. Users are advised to disable auto-updates until the company confirms no malicious versions were published.
